leads.text: SSRF via unvalidated HTTP redirect following in `_http_get` (src/picklescan/scanner.py:250-267). On a 302 response the function recursively calls itself with the fully server-controlled `Location` response header: `if response.status == 302: return _http_get(response.headers["Location"])` (line 262). The recursive invocation then does `conn = http.client.HTTPSConnection(parsed_url.netloc)` (line 256) and `conn.request("GET", path_and_query)` (line 258) against that attacker-supplied netloc, with NO host/IP allowlist, no scheme validation, no private/link-local address filter, and no redirect-count cap. `_http_get` is reached from two entry points: `scan_url(url)` (line 628: `scan_bytes(io.BytesIO(_http_get(url)), url)`) and `scan_huggingface_model(repo_id)` (line 578 and line 589: `io.BytesIO(_http_get(url))`), both wired to CLI flags `-u/--url` and `-hf/--huggingface` (cli.py:66, cli.py:68). Any server the scanner is pointed at -- or any HuggingFace-hosted model repo, since HF legitimately 302-redirects LFS files to a CDN, which is why this redirect support exists -- can redirect picklescan to an arbitrary internal host, e.g. `Location: https://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/` or an internal admin service. Note also that the parsed scheme is discarded: `HTTPSConnection` is used unconditionally on whatever netloc the redirect supplies. The fetched body is then parsed/scanned and partially reflected into logs and the `ScanResult`, giving a response-content oracle.

leads.text: Unbounded recursion / stack-exhaustion DoS in `_http_get` (src/picklescan/scanner.py:250-267). The 302 handler at line 262 recurses via `return _http_get(response.headers["Location"])` with no depth counter, no visited-URL set, and no maximum-redirect parameter -- the function's only parameter is `url`. A malicious or compromised server (or a redirect loop reached through `scan_url`/`scan_huggingface_model`) that answers every request with `302 Location: <self>` drives infinite mutual recursion until Python's recursion limit is hit, raising RecursionError; each frame also holds an un-closed `HTTPSConnection`, so sockets/file descriptors accumulate across the ~1000 frames before unwinding. I verified by query that no `max_redirect`-style guard exists anywhere under src/.

leads.text: Path traversal / Zip-Slip in `scan_7z_bytes` (src/picklescan/scanner.py:428-447). Archive member names are taken straight from the untrusted 7z file -- `file_names = archive.getnames()` (line 438) -- and the ONLY filter applied is a suffix test, `targets = [f for f in file_names if f.endswith(tuple(_pickle_file_extensions))]` (line 439). That attacker-controlled `targets` list is then passed to `archive.extract(path=tmpdir, targets=targets)` (line 442), which writes to disk, and each name is re-joined as `file_path = os.path.join(tmpdir, file_name)` (line 444) before `os.path.isfile(file_path)` (446) and `scan_file_path(file_path)` (447). There is no containment validation of any kind between the archive and the extract/join -- no normpath, no realpath, no commonpath, and no `startswith(tmpdir)` check; I confirmed by query that the only path-normalization call in the whole of src/ is an unrelated `os.path.abspath(args.path)` in cli.py:58. A 7z entry named e.g. `../../../../home/victim/.bashrc.pkl` or `..\..\..\startup\x.pkl` satisfies the `.pkl` suffix filter and escapes the TemporaryDirectory on extraction, yielding arbitrary file write (and, via os.path.join, scanning/leaking of files outside tmpdir into the ScanResult). Exploitable through `scan_file_path`/`scan_directory_path` on any attacker-supplied `.7z`, and reached automatically from `scan_pytorch` line 525 (`_is_7z_file(data)` -> `scan_7z_bytes(data, file_id)`). Severity depends partly on whether the installed py7zr version sanitizes member names, but picklescan itself adds no defense.

leads.text: `RelaxedZipFile.open` (src/picklescan/relaxed_zipfile.py:19-88) is a near-verbatim copy of CPython's `zipfile.ZipFile.open` with the local-header/central-directory filename consistency check deliberately removed, creating a zip-name-confusion detection-evasion primitive. The method reads and validates the local file header -- `fheader = zef_file.read(sizeFileHeader)` (77), `len(fheader) != sizeFileHeader` -> BadZipFile (78-79), `struct.unpack` (80), `fheader[_FH_SIGNATURE] != stringFileHeader` -> BadZipFile (81-82) -- then reads the local filename and extra field (`zef_file.read(fheader[_FH_FILENAME_LENGTH])` at 84, `zef_file.read(fheader[_FH_EXTRA_FIELD_LENGTH])` at 86) and proceeds directly to `zipfile.ZipExtFile(zef_file, mode, zinfo, pwd, True)` (88). Upstream CPython compares the decoded local filename against `zinfo.orig_filename` and raises `BadZipFile('File name in directory %r and header %r differ.')`; that comparison is absent here -- the bytes read at line 84 are discarded without any equality test. Because `scan_zip_bytes` selects which members to scan from the central directory (`file_names = zip.namelist()` at scanner.py:458, then `zip.open(file_name, "r")` at 462/468/473), an attacker can craft a PyTorch/zip model whose central directory advertises a benign name while the local header names a different member, so picklescan's view of the archive diverges from that of a real consumer using its own zip reader (torch's miniz). Compounding it, scanner.py:464-466 only scans a member if its extension is in `_pickle_file_extensions` or `magic_bytes.startswith(mn)` matches `_pickle_magic_bytes`/`_numpy_magic_bytes`, so a member that evades both gates is silently skipped. Net effect: a malicious pickle can be delivered inside a zip that picklescan reports as clean. Lower-ranked because the relaxation is intentional (the class is named RelaxedZipFile, to tolerate torch-produced archives), so this is a design-tradeoff weakness rather than an oversight.

leads.text: Unsanitized `repo_id` and remote-controlled `file_name` interpolated into request URLs in `scan_huggingface_model` (src/picklescan/scanner.py:574-590). The entry-point parameter `repo_id` is spliced raw into `_http_get(f"https://huggingface.co/api/models/{repo_id}")` (line 578) with no validation, URL-encoding, or character allowlist; the JSON response is then mined for `sibling.get("rfilename")` values (line 579) which are spliced -- also unsanitized -- into `url = f"https://huggingface.co/{repo_id}/resolve/main/{file_name}"` (line 588) and fetched via `io.BytesIO(_http_get(url))` (line 589). Because the literal prefix already contains a `/`, `urlparse` pins netloc to huggingface.co, so this is URL path/query injection rather than direct host control: a `repo_id` containing `../`, `?`, or `#` can traverse to or reshape a different HuggingFace API endpoint, and a server-supplied `rfilename` (a value the model publisher controls) can do the same on the resolve path. The practical impact is that it widens lead #1 -- an injected path can steer the request to an endpoint whose 302 `Location` the attacker influences, and `_http_get` then follows that redirect to an arbitrary host with no allowlist. Ranked lowest of the five because exploitation requires chaining through the redirect weakness to reach a security boundary.

leads.text: `scan_directory_path` — the function behind the primary CLI mode `picklescan -p <dir>` — gates which files get scanned on an extension allowlist that OMITS `_numpy_file_extensions`. The condition at scanner.py:604-606 is `if file_ext not in _zip_file_extensions and file_ext not in _pickle_file_extensions and file_ext not in _pytorch_file_extensions: continue`. Since `_numpy_file_extensions = {".npy"}` (line 217) is absent from that test, and `.npy` is in none of the three sets checked (`_zip_file_extensions = {".zip", ".npz", ".7z"}`, `_pickle_file_extensions = {".pkl", ".pickle", ".joblib", ".dat", ".data"}`, `_pytorch_file_extensions = {".bin", ".pt", ".pth", ".ckpt"}`), every bare `.npy` file in a scanned directory tree is silently `continue`d and never scanned. This is an absence of coverage, not a dataflow bug: the capability to scan `.npy` exists and is wired up everywhere else — a dedicated `scan_numpy` method exists (line 482), `scan_bytes` explicitly dispatches `.npy` to it (`if file_ext is not None and file_ext in _numpy_file_extensions: return scan_numpy(...)`), and `scan_zip_bytes` scans `.npy` members found inside archives (line 471). Only the recursive directory walk omits it. A `.npy` holding an object-dtype array embeds a pickle that executes on `np.load(path, allow_pickle=True)`, so a repository containing a malicious `.npy` is reported with `Scanned files` not counting it and `issues_count == 0`, making the CLI exit 0 ("clean").

leads.text:
`scan_zip_bytes`'s content-sniffing fallback cannot recognise pickle protocol 0 or 1, so those payloads evade scanning entirely when the archive member's extension is not in `_pickle_file_extensions`. The gate at scanner.py:466 is `if file_ext in _pickle_file_extensions or any(magic_bytes.startswith(mn) for mn in _pickle_magic_bytes)`, and `_pickle_magic_bytes = {b"\x80\x00", b"\x80\x01", b"\x80\x02", b"\x80\x03", b"\x80\x04", b"\x80\x05"}` (line 223) only matches the PROTO opcode framing emitted by protocol 2+. Protocol 0/1 pickles carry no `\x80` prefix — they begin directly with an opcode byte such as `c` (GLOBAL), `(` (MARK), `}` or `]`. Consequently a zip/pytorch archive member named e.g. `config.json`, `README.md`, `tokenizer.model` or `model.safetensors` whose body is a protocol-0 pickle satisfies neither branch and is skipped without even a warning. The repository's own test corpus proves protocol-0 payloads are live threats rather than theoretical: `tests/init_data_files.py` writes `data/malicious0.pkl` as raw bytes beginning `b'c__builtin__
globals
...'` and `data/malicious10.pkl` as `b"(S'raise RuntimeError("Injection running")'
i__builtin__
exec
."` — both are unframed, both execute, and both would be invisible here. Note `scan_zip_bytes` is a reachable chokepoint (centrality 0.00119, reachable_from_entry = true) reached from every archive-bearing input path.

leads.text: `RelaxedZipFile.open` deliberately disables the ZIP integrity and header-consistency checks that stock `zipfile.ZipFile.open` performs, and it is the reader used for every archive picklescan inspects. src/picklescan/relaxed_zipfile.py defines RelaxedZipFile.open as a copy of CPython's zipfile.ZipFile.open with the archive-integrity protections deliberately removed — the class name itself announces the relaxation, and it is the live ZIP reader for the scanner. Three stdlib checks are absent: (a) CRC verification is explicitly disabled at line 91 via `zef._expected_crc = None`; (b) the local-file-header vs central-directory filename equality check (`if fname_str != zinfo.orig_filename: raise BadZipFile('File name in directory %r and header %r differ.')`) is gone; (c) the general-purpose flag-bit checks (bit 5 compressed-patch, bit 6 strong-encryption) are gone. Queries for the identifiers `flag_bits` and `orig_filename` return ZERO rows anywhere in the scan. The retained checks are only truncation (line 78) and the PK\003\004 magic (line 81), after which control flows straight to `zipfile.ZipExtFile(zef_file, mode, zinfo, pwd, True)` at line 88. Because the member is located purely by the central-directory `zinfo.header_offset` (line 68) with the local header's own filename read and discarded (line 84), the scanner and a downstream loader that honours local headers can resolve the same archive to different bytes — a scanner/loader parser differential that lets a crafted ZIP present benign content to picklescan while a consumer deserializes a different member. Disabling CRC also removes the last integrity signal that the bytes scanned are the bytes stored.

leads.text: The literal _pickle_magic_bytes = {b"\x80\x00", b"\x80\x01", b"\x80\x02", b"\x80\x03", b"\x80\x04", b"\x80\x05"} (line 223) only enumerates the pickle PROTO opcode (0x80), which is emitted exclusively by pickle protocols 2-5. Therefore a malicious PROTOCOL-0 or PROTOCOL-1 pickle placed in a .zip/.npz under an extension outside _pickle_file_extensions (e.g. `data.bin`, `model.pt`, `notes.txt`, no extension) matches neither branch and is silently skipped — never passed to scan_pickle_bytes. The scanner's own parser handles these protocols fine (_list_globals explicitly dispatches on the proto-0/1 `GLOBAL` and `INST` opcodes), so the gap is purely in the magic-byte literal, not the parser. Corroborating: the entry `b"\x80\x00"` is dead weight (pickle never emits PROTO 0), showing the set was authored as "the PROTO opcode" and protocol 0/1 framing was simply not considered.

Consequence: a global `builtins __import__` is classified only SafetyLevel.Suspicious, which does NOT increment issues_count in _build_scan_result_from_raw_globals and therefore does not mark the file infected or drive a non-zero CLI exit. leads.text: Components-with-known-vulnerabilities enumeration (no request flow needed). The declared Dependency set for this scan is exactly 11 pinned entries: aiohttp==3.13.3, black==24.10.0, cloudpickle==3.1.1, flake8==5.0.4, numpy>1.24.0,<2.0.0, py7zr==0.22.0, pytest==8.3.5, pytest-cov==6.0.0, requests==2.32.5, torch==2.8.0, twine==4.0.1. Flagged as outdated / end-of-life and warranting advisory-database confirmation by the verifier: (a) `numpy>1.24.0,<2.0.0` — the constraint pins the resolver to the NumPy 1.x series, which is end-of-life (1.26.4 was the final 1.x release); (b) `twine==4.0.1` — a 2022-era release, many major versions behind; (c) `flake8==5.0.4` — likewise a 2022-era release. Note the runtime attack surface these feed: py7zr parses attacker-supplied .7z archives in scan_7z_bytes and numpy parses attacker-supplied .npy/.npz in scan_numpy, both reachable entry points, so an archive/array-parser CVE in those two is directly attacker-reachable via a hostile model file. I could not query a CVE/advisory database with the two read-only graph tools available, so I am asserting only the declared versions (which I queried) and the outdated/EOL status — specific CVE IDs must be re-derived by the verifier against an advisory feed.
